name: Gareth Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth Chen, forty-three. I have a bachelor's in accounting, but I'm a junior at Cedar Tax after changing careers, still learning the job and paid at the low end. I enter small-trader records and prepare tax returns, then ask my supervisor to check what I got wrong. I use a paper checklist and never use AI tools.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making a trader's messy book make sense, even if it takes me longer than the others. I dislike the late filing rush and the feeling I slow everyone down. My partner Leila drives buses, our two children are nine and twelve, and we have a mortgage. We have less than one month of expenses saved, and there are few other accounting firms near our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like nothing much happening at our firm. The partners already have a receipt sorter, but I still work from the paper checklist because I have not learned the AI part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other juniors that somebody still has to check a tax return before it goes out. I'd tell friends the new tools should make the work less rushed, not give the partners an excuse to hold wages down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the ordinary month worries me more than the software here. I'm forty-three, only a junior after changing careers, and the pay is low. Leila and I have less than one month's bills saved, a mortgage and two children at school, while similar accounting jobs are scarce nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing the small-trader returns with my paper checklist and ask my supervisor to check the hard ones. This week I'd call the lender about moving our payment date after Leila's bus-driver payday. In the first year of a plateau I'd keep the children's school lunches paid and put twenty a month aside only if the new payment date stops the overdraft fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even if my job stays. The mortgage can still be late when two wages land on the wrong days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the last mortgage payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month our mortgage payment left the account two days before Leila's wages came in. We paid an overdraft fee and borrowed from the grocery money. A small AI saving cannot move a bank date for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lender for a date after the fifteenth, when the bus company pays Leila. If they refuse, I'd keep the fee in the budget and cut our Friday takeaway. I won't count twenty pounds saved until the account actually holds it.

say: I would defend **human checks** on every tax return.
I would ask that saved time ease **wage pressure**.
think: The **mortgage timing** already costs us overdraft fees when my partner’s wages arrive late.
My **junior pay** and few nearby jobs leave little room.
do: Keep the **paper checklist** on small-trader returns.
Call the **lender** to move the payment date.
Save **twenty monthly** only if the new date prevents fees.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the mortgage despite stable work.
S0.quote: A small AI saving cannot move a bank date for me.
fieldNote: The **payment-date mismatch** and less than one month saved make baseline finances fragile.
He remains a **junior accountant** at forty-three and relies on manual checks rather than AI.

steps.text: Keep paper checklist and supervisor review for difficult tax returns
Ask lender to move mortgage payment after bus-driver payday
Save twenty monthly only if changed date prevents overdraft fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking are nearly my whole desk. If the tool does both, I cannot see why the partners would keep many juniors, especially someone still learning like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask the union to see the staffing plan before another junior leaves. I'd tell friends the savings should come with paid training and a wage floor, because families cannot live on a promise of a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could be cut within a year or two. I have a bachelor's in accounting, but I returned to this field late and still make mistakes that my supervisor catches. A firm with two juniors might keep the faster one, and there are few other desks near home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take last month's correction notes to my supervisor and ask for two paid hours a week to improve on the work I get wrong. I'd join the union branch meeting this month and ask about a rule for retraining before hours are cut. If they cut me anyway, I'd apply for the vacant accounts-clerk post at the local clinic only if its pay covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can picture the hours on my payslip shrinking, and there is no savings pot to hold the house up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children notice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our youngest, Ava, needs new shoes next term and the older one, Leo, has a school trip. I'd tell them the trip can wait before I tell them the house might be at risk. I don't want my children doing mortgage arithmetic at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistakes would paid training address?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor circled three wrong tax codes last month. I'd ask her to work through those with me in paid time, not after closing. If the firm will not do that, the clinic vacancy may be my bridge, but it is one post and might close.

say: I would seek **staffing plans** through the union before the partners remove junior hours.
I would demand **paid learning** before junior hours disappear.
think: My **hours** could shrink soon because AI does routine checks.
Few **nearby desks** weaken my chance of replacing the income.
do: Request **two paid hours** weekly to fix tax-code errors.
Attend the **union meeting** on retraining before cuts.
Apply for the **clinic vacancy** only if pay covers mortgage.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing pay needed for our house.
S1.quote: I don't want my children doing mortgage arithmetic at the dinner table.
fieldNote: The **correction notes** make his junior standing concrete, even though he has an accounting degree.
He expects **reduced hours** before dismissal and ties any clinic move to a mortgage-covering salary.

steps.text: Study tax-code errors with supervisor if firm grants two paid hours weekly
Attend union branch meeting about staffing and retraining
Apply for vacant clinic clerk post if pay covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 gives me almost no time to become good at a job that may vanish. A better, cheaper thinker would be doing the returns before I finished learning this firm's files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government must guarantee a wage bridge and stop firms from cutting staff without notice. At work I'd ask the union to make the partners put dates and numbers on any plan, not just say people matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior accounting post to go in the first year after full AGI arrives in 2028. My job is at a desk, so robots around 2031 give me no extra years. Leila's bus wage will not cover the mortgage, school meals and bills by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop the Friday takeaway and hold the forty a month in cash. I'd ask the union about notice and apply for the open school office post if its salary covers the mortgage and it is funded. In the first year after 2028, if I lose this job, I'd claim wage support at once and ask the lender for a temporary payment arrangement before missing an instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and tired. I have a list of calls, but none of them makes a new wage appear by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila the truth before the children hear a rumour from school. She could ask for another bus shift, but the depot cannot promise one every week. I would not build a mortgage plan on overtime that has not been offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lender gets a call before a missed payment, not after the letter arrives. I'd bring the payslip, the mortgage statement and any benefit decision. If the school role has closed, I'd ask the office manager about the next funded vacancy while taking any temporary work I can get.

say: I would demand **wage support** and notice before job cuts.
I would ask the union for **dated staffing plans**.
think: My **junior desk post** may go soon after 2028.
One **bus-driver wage** cannot cover our mortgage and children.
do: Stop **Friday takeaways** and hold forty cash monthly.
Seek **mortgage-covering funded school work**; if the vacancy closes, ask about the next funded opening and take temporary work.
Claim **wage support** and ask lender for temporary terms after dismissal.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the likely loss of my wage.
S2.quote: I would not build a mortgage plan on overtime that has not been offered.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his desk work in 2028; the later robot date gives no delay.
His **bus-driver fallback** is uncertain because extra shifts are not guaranteed, so lender support remains urgent.

steps.text: Stop Friday takeaway and hold forty monthly in cash
Apply for funded school office vacancy if salary covers mortgage
Seek wage support and lender terms after 2028 dismissal before missing mortgage payment
After job loss, seek next funded school opening and temporary work if vacancy closes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years sounds better, but the mortgage is due every month of those five years. If I spend them waiting, I will reach 2031 with the same thin savings and fewer junior jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm and government should pay for a real route into new work, not hand out leaflets. I'd ask the union for training places and income cover while people study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into payroll at the school district before 2031, though that is screen work too and not safe forever. My accounting degree helps, but I would need to learn the district's rules and get a funded opening. Robots in 2034 do not extend my accounting desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in the district payroll course this year only if the firm pays the two-hundred fee and gives paid study hours. I'd ask my union representative to negotiate those hours and shadow one payroll close if the district grants access. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my return post ends, I'd apply for a funded school payroll vacancy only if its wage covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years gives me a route to test, but paying bills during that time still keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two hundred is more than the cash we have left most months. I'd put the fee and paid hours in one written request. If refused, I'd ask the union about free district workshops and keep my current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the payroll visit useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to see an actual payroll close, including a correction when a worker's hours were wrong. A certificate alone will not convince a district manager to hire a forty-eight-year-old junior. I'd ask for a supervisor to sign off on the visit.

say: I would seek **paid training** and income cover during a move into another job.
I would reject **leaflets** as a job plan.
think: A **payroll role** may be a bridge, but its screen work is exposed too.
My **thin cash** makes unpaid study unrealistic.
do: Enrol in **payroll study** if fee and paid hours are funded.
Ask the **union** for paid shadowing at a payroll close.
Apply after 2031 for a **funded payroll vacancy** if wage covers mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills during a slow transition.
S3.quote: A certificate alone will not convince a district manager to hire a forty-eight-year-old junior.
fieldNote: The **two-hundred fee** exceeds his spare cash, so funded study and paid hours are required.
A **payroll close** would test an alternative role, but he knows it is still screen work.

steps.text: Enrol in district payroll course if firm funds fee and paid hours
Ask union to negotiate paid district payroll shadowing
Apply for funded school payroll vacancy after 2031 if wage covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time for our children; they would be nearly grown by 2036. I still have to get through next month's mortgage before I can think about the end of the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm to keep a paid path for people who entered accounting late. I'd ask the union to push for shorter hours without losing the wage that keeps households in their homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My return-preparation work is still likely to go when thinking AI arrives in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not protect that desk, but ten years could let me move to school administration and pay down some mortgage. I do not think I will become a technology expert overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the paper checklist now and ask the school district next spring about a paid office apprenticeship for adults, only if the pay covers our mortgage. I'd join if it has a funded place and supervised hours, and I would keep the family budget tight while I learn. In the first year after 2036, if my tax work ends, I'd take the district role only if a funded vacancy still exists; otherwise I'd claim wage support and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though a decade feels like a chance. The children will need us for years before they earn their own money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you expect from your children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo would be twenty-two by then and Ava nineteen, but I do not want to make my grown children the emergency fund. I'd rather use the years to keep the mortgage current and find work with a real payslip. I would tell them they can choose school without carrying our debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which apprenticeship terms matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the apprenticeship wage and the final office wage cover the mortgage, and whether the place is actually funded. If either answer is no, I cannot move yet. I would keep my current contract and ask again when a funded post opens.

say: I would seek a **paid path** for late entrants.
I would ask for **shorter hours** without lost household pay.
think: My **return work** still faces AGI in 2036.
A **school office** route needs a funded wage, not hope.
do: Start a **funded adult apprenticeship** only with paid supervised hours and training and final wages covering the mortgage.
Keep my **current contract** and checklist if apprenticeship terms fail; ask again when funded posts open.
After **2036 job loss**, take funded mortgage-covering district work or claim support and keep searching if none exists.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though a decade offers a route.
S4.quote: I do not want to make my grown children the emergency fund.
fieldNote: His **school-age children** will be adults by 2036, yet he refuses to shift mortgage risk onto them.
The **apprenticeship route** requires funded places, supervised hours and a wage sufficient for the mortgage.

steps.text: Start funded paid supervised adult office apprenticeship if training and final wages cover mortgage
Keep current contract and paper checklist if apprenticeship terms fail; await funded opening
Take funded district role after 2036 tax job ends if vacancy exists and wage covers mortgage
Claim support and keep searching if tax role ends after 2036 without funded district vacancy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I am only just learning a desk job that might disappear. A wage bridge, a lender willing to change terms, and paid training tied to a funded vacancy would help. My partner's bus shifts keep us going, but overtime is not a mortgage plan. I need time that comes with a payslip.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how it feels to start again at forty-three. My children see me doing homework at the kitchen table, and I want that to mean effort can lead somewhere. If the first rung goes, I need more than a cheerful speech about adapting.

headlineQuote: My partner's bus shifts keep us going, but overtime is not a mortgage plan.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Gareth is a junior accountant at Cedar Tax after changing careers.
His **accounting bachelor’s** has not yet made him skilled or well paid in the role.
He uses **no AI**, relying on a paper checklist and supervisor corrections.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and less than one month saved make even a plateau worrying.
Few **nearby firms** limit his options, so he seeks union support and funded moves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior desk job before his household can build savings.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **wage bridge**, lender flexibility and paid training linked to funded vacancies.
